area: Area IX. Performance and Ground Reference Maneuvers
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain the chandelle's two halves, its aerodynamics and its energy plan, demonstrate one each way from the right seat while explaining it (about 30° of bank, wings level at the 180° point ±10°, just above a stall airspeed, no lower than 1,500 feet AGL), and spot and fix the errors your commercial learners will make.
why: A chandelle is a maximum performance 180° climbing turn that ends wings level, nose high, just above stall speed [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. Performance maneuvers like it build control smoothness, maneuver planning, situational awareness and division of attention [[24:210|AFH 10-1]]. As the instructor you teach a maneuver that deliberately runs the airspeed down near the stall with high power, so you need to see trouble coming early, explain it in plain words and keep the airplane safe while a learner flies it.

prereading.what: The chandelle: the two halves, entry, power, rudder in left and right chandelles, the finish and the 14 common errors. Read it twice.
prereading.label: AFH 10-4 to 10-6

prereading.what: Bank classes, adverse yaw and the rudder, slip and skid, rate and radius of turn, overbanking.
prereading.label: AFH 3-12 to 3-14

prereading.what: Climbs and climbing turns: P-factor and torque, pitch as the speed decays, why steep banks hurt the climb, level-off.
prereading.label: AFH 3-19 to 3-20

prereading.what: Controls near the critical angle of attack, stall cues, power-on stalls, accelerated stalls, VA and VO, the cross-control stall.
prereading.label: AFH 5-11 to 5-20

prereading.what: Left-turning tendencies, load factor and stall speed, VA and its limits, and the PHAK's note on chandelles.
prereading.label: PHAK 5-31 to 5-37

prereading.what: Energy management: total energy, energy exchange, and the throttle and elevator as energy controls.
prereading.label: AFH 4-1 to 4-4

prereading.what: Demonstrating while explaining, guarding the controls, distractions, see and avoid, and correcting learner errors.
prereading.label: AIH 9-7 to 9-12

warmup: Think first: your commercial learner finishes a left chandelle with the wings level, but the heading is 30° short, the stall horn is steady and the ball is well to the right. Three things went wrong at once. Which one came first, which single moment in the maneuver would have shown you it was coming, and what one sentence would you say on the next try?

key_terms.def: A maximum performance 180° climbing turn from about straight-and-level flight to a wings-level, nose-high attitude just above stall speed [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
The hinge of the maneuver: the end of the constant-bank, rising-pitch half and the start of the constant-pitch, rolling-out half [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
A slow, coordinated, steady reduction of bank from the 90° point so the wings come level exactly at the 180° point [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
The stall speed with power applied. The chandelle ends just above it, with the nose-high attitude held for a moment [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].
The rising wing gets more lift and more drag, so the nose yaws opposite to the direction of the roll; rudder in the direction of the roll cancels it [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].
At a high angle of attack the downward-moving propeller blade takes a bigger bite, moving the center of thrust right and yawing the nose left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].
The outside wing travels a longer path, flies faster and makes more lift, so the bank tends to steepen; in a chandelle it grows as airspeed drops [[24:75|AFH 3-14]] [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

The highest speed at which the design limit load can be imposed by gusts or full one-sided deflection of one control without damage. It goes down as weight goes down [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].
A historical limitation on certain airplanes: the highest speed at which, at any given weight, full control travel will not exceed the design limit load factor [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
Any stall at more than +1 G, as in a turn or pull-up, so it comes at a higher indicated airspeed than the 1 G stall [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
The AFH's name for the elevator: it moves energy between altitude and airspeed. The throttle is the total energy controller [[24:90|AFH 4-4]].

chunks.title: Purpose, procedure and the CFI standard

body.p: Purpose: the chandelle asks for the most altitude possible for the bank and power chosen, but it is not judged on the altitude gained. It is judged on how well the pilot gets maximum climb performance for that bank and power, and on the skill shown [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. Performance maneuvers in general build flight control application, maneuver planning, situational awareness and division of attention, with pressures, attitudes and airspeeds that keep changing [[24:210|AFH 10-1]].

Procedure in one breath: flaps and gear up, clear the area, enter from straight-and-level flight or a shallow dive at the manufacturer's speed (often VA or VO), roll to about 30°, then add power and raise the nose at a constant rate so the highest pitch arrives at 90°. Hold that pitch and roll out at a constant rate to wings level at 180°, just above the power-on stall speed, hold it a moment, then lower the nose [[24:214|AFH 10-5]] [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

head: What the examiner sees
CFI ACS standard
rows: Select an altitude that allows the maneuver to be performed no lower than 1,500 feet above ground level (AGL) (ACS AI.IX.C.S2)
Establish the appropriate entry configuration, power, and airspeed (ACS AI.IX.C.S3)
Establish the angle of bank at approximately 30° (ACS AI.IX.C.S4)
Simultaneously apply power and pitch to maintain a smooth, coordinated climbing turn, in either direction, to the 90° point, with a constant bank and continuously decreasing airspeed (ACS AI.IX.C.S5)
Begin a coordinated constant rate rollout from the 90° point to the 180° point maintaining power and a constant pitch attitude (ACS AI.IX.C.S6)
Complete rollout at the 180° point, ±10° just above a stall airspeed, and maintaining that airspeed momentarily avoiding a stall (ACS AI.IX.C.S7)
Resume a straight-and-level flight with minimum loss of altitude (ACS AI.IX.C.S8)
Analyze and correct common errors related to this Task (ACS AI.IX.C.S9)

body.p: What is new for you: the skills line says the applicant 'demonstrates and simultaneously explains', and S9 means the examiner may fly a flawed chandelle as your learner. Skills S1 to S8 use the same words as the commercial ACS your learners fly to (ACS CA.V.C.S1 to S8). The private ACS has no chandelle Task, so the learners you teach it to are working toward the commercial ACS. For the general demonstration-performance method and the exchange of controls, see the Steep Turns lesson (AI.IX.A); this lesson uses them only where the chandelle needs something special.

callout.text: For ASEL, the evaluator must select at least four Area IX Tasks, including Task A or B, Task C or D, and Tasks E and F (ACS Area IX note). Prepare both Chandelles and Lazy Eights.

check.q: Which numbers does the CFI ACS give for the chandelle, and which numbers does it leave out?
check.a: Approximately 30° of bank, the 180° point ±10°, and no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (ACS AI.IX.C.S2, S4, S7). It gives no pitch, no entry speed and no altitude gain; the AFH judges climb performance for the bank and power used [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

chunks.title: The two halves: constant bank, then constant pitch

body.p: The AFH teaches the chandelle as two 90° phases. First 90°: constant bank and continuously increasing pitch. Second 90°: constant pitch and continuously decreasing bank [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. That is the sentence your learner should be able to say back to you before the engine starts.

head: Phase
What is held
What changes
What decides success
rows: Pitch rises at a rate that puts maximum pitch exactly at 90° [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]
The pitch reached at 90°: too low and the speed never comes down to just above the stall; too high and it may stall before the end [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]
Bank comes out at a slow, constant rate [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]
The rollout rate: too fast or too sluggish and the turn goes past 180° or is not complete when the wings are level [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]
Airspeed just above the power-on stall speed [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]

body.p: Teaching it: learners mix the halves up. A common picture is 'the nose keeps coming up all the way around', which is listed error 6, letting the pitch rise during the rollout [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]. Another is rolling out early because the bank feels uncomfortable, error 7 [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]. Give each half one job and one word: 'pitch' for the first, 'roll' for the second (application).

callout.text: On the ground, have the learner pick two references before the flight lesson: one off the wingtip for 90° and one behind for 180°. In the air, ask 'where is your 90° point?' before every entry (application).
First half: bank still, nose moving. Second half: nose still, wings moving.

check.q: A learner's airspeed is still 15 knots above the stall at 180°, with the wings level on heading. Which half do you debrief, and why?
check.a: The first half: the pitch set by the 90° point was too low, so the airspeed never decreased to just above the stall [[24:213|AFH 10-4]] [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

chunks.title: Configuration and entry for a maximum performance climb

body.p: Appropriate airplane configuration for maximum performance climb: flaps and retractable gear up before the chandelle [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. Enter from straight-and-level flight or a shallow dive at the manufacturer's recommended airspeed, in many cases VA or VO [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

bullets: Bank: generally 30°, rolled in smoothly and coordinated after the entry speed is set [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].
Pitch and power together: smooth back pressure at a constant rate while increasing power to the recommended setting [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].
Fixed-pitch propeller: set the throttle so as not to exceed rpm limits [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].
Constant-speed propeller: normal cruise or climb power, as appropriate; advance the propeller control before increasing power [[24:214|AFH 10-5]] [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].
Normally aspirated engines lose power as altitude increases, so the throttle keeps moving forward to hold the climb setting [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

body.p: Why only about 30°? In a climbing turn some lift turns the airplane, so the climb is shallower; steep banks significantly decrease the rate of climb, and a medium or steep bank can degrade climb performance or leave none [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]. The chandelle bank is the compromise between turning 180° and climbing. The AFH lists both extremes as errors: too shallow ends in a stall, too steep fails to get maximum performance [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

callout.text: Figure 10-3 says to apply full power without exceeding limits, while the AFH text says the recommended setting, which for a constant-speed propeller may be cruise or climb power [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. Teach your airplane's POH setting and say which one you use.
Ground brief item: today's weight, VA or the POH entry speed for that weight, the power setting and the rpm limit. A learner who knows these numbers before takeoff flies S3 instead of guessing it.

check.q: Your learner asks why the chandelle does not use 45° of bank to turn faster. What do you say?
check.a: Steep banks significantly decrease the rate of climb [[24:81|AFH 3-20]], and an initial bank that is too steep fails to get maximum performance [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

chunks.title: Maintaining coordinated flight: adverse yaw and left-turning tendencies

body.p: Maintaining coordinated flight is the chandelle's hardest feet job. When the ailerons roll the airplane, the rising wing gets more lift and drag and the nose yaws opposite to the roll. Rudder with the aileron, in the direction of the roll, cancels that adverse yaw [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

On top of adverse yaw come the left-turning tendencies. In a climb the center of propeller thrust moves right (P-factor) and torque rolls the airplane left, so right rudder and aileron pressures are needed [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. The corkscrew slipstream is strongest at high propeller speed and low forward speed [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]], and built-in compensation is set for cruise speed [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]. A chandelle ends at exactly the wrong combination: high power, high angle of attack, low speed.

head: Moment
What yaws the nose
Rudder the AFH describes
rows: P-factor and other left-turning tendencies have greater effect [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]
Left adverse yaw plus left-turning tendencies [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]
Significant right rudder near the end [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]
A yawing moment to the right partly cancels the left-turning tendencies [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]
Very little left rudder, or less right rudder, depending on the airplane [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]

body.p: How the pilot knows: sense the slip or skid in the seat, glance at the ball, and use the control pressures needed [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. A skid presses you to the outside of the turn and a slip to the inside [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].

callout.text: Teaching line (application): 'Every time the airspeed drops 10 knots, add a little more right rudder. On a left chandelle, the rollout needs the most right rudder of all. On a right chandelle, the rollout gives some of it back.'

check.q: Why does a left chandelle's rollout need more right rudder than a right chandelle's?
check.a: Rolling right out of a left turn adds left adverse yaw to the left-turning tendencies; rolling left out of a right turn yaws the nose right, which partly cancels them [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

chunks.title: Overbanking tendencies as the speed decays

body.p: Overbanking tendencies: in a turn the outside wing travels a longer path in the same time, so it flies faster and makes more lift, and the bank tends to steepen unless opposite aileron is used [[24:75|AFH 3-14]]. The difference grows as the turn radius gets smaller [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].

In ordinary flight a medium bank (about 20° to 45°) holds itself with neutral aileron [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]. The chandelle is different: as airspeed decreases, the overbanking tendency increases, so proper aileron use keeps the bank fixed until the rollout starts at 90° [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. Figure 10-3 says 'neutralize ailerons' right after the roll-in [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]; that is true at the start, but expect to need a little opposite aileron as the speed bleeds off.

bullets: What you see: the bank creeping from 30° toward 40° halfway to 90°. It is listed error 4, letting the bank increase after it is set [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].
Why it matters: more bank turns the airplane faster at the same speed [[24:75|AFH 3-14]], so the learner reaches 90° early with speed to spare, and more bank cuts the climb [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].
How to fix it: a sight picture of the wing against the horizon at 30°, a quick attitude indicator check, and the cue 'hold the bank, it wants to roll in' (application).

callout.text: The bank steepening near the stall is not just a heading problem. Slow and steepening is the setup for a stall at a higher speed than the learner expects, because load factor and stall speed rise with bank [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].

check.q: Figure 10-3 says to neutralize the ailerons after rolling in. Why might your learner still need opposite aileron before the 90° point?
check.a: As airspeed decreases the overbanking tendency increases, so aileron is needed to keep the bank fixed until the rollout begins [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

chunks.title: Maneuvering speed, weight and accelerated stalls

body.p: Maneuvering speed, including the impact of weight changes: at or below VA or VO the airplane reaches the critical angle of attack and unloads the wing before it can exceed the design load limit; above them, it can reach the limit load first [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. VA goes down with weight, for example 100 knots heavily loaded but only 90 knots light [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]. VO, where published, applies at any given weight [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

bullets: VA must be in the AFM/POH of recently designed airplanes; for older ones the PHAK's rough guide is 1.7 times the normal stall speed [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].
VA protects one full input, one time, in one axis, in smooth air, not several full inputs or inputs in more than one axis [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].
The PHAK puts the recommended chandelle entry speed generally near the design maneuvering speed [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].
Application: a commercial learner who briefs the max-weight VA on a light day plans an entry that is too fast for the actual weight.

body.p: Accelerated stalls: a stall at more than +1 G, from a turn, a pull-up or another abrupt change in flightpath, at a higher indicated airspeed than the 1 G stall [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. Application: a level 30° bank is about 1.15 G, so a 50-knot 1 G stall becomes about 54 knots; a hard pull adds more.

This is why the pull-up must be smooth. A chandelle pull-up of more than 2 G will not gain as much altitude, and in a low-powered airplane may give a net loss; the smoothest pull-up with a moderate load factor gains the most [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]]. Stalls from abrupt maneuvers tend to be more aggressive, can come at a higher speed or lower pitch than expected, and without an immediate recovery may lead to a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

callout.text: Teach the pull as a slow count, not a grab: the AFH says smooth back pressure at a constant rate [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. If you feel a learner yank, take note of the seat pressure; load factor is judged by seat feel, not by control force [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

check.q: A learner yanks the nose up at the entry and gets buffet at a speed well above the normal stall. What happened, and what does the PHAK say about the altitude?
check.a: An accelerated stall: more than 1 G raises the stall speed [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. A pull-up over 2 G also gains less altitude, or even loses it in a low-powered airplane [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

chunks.title: Pitch control as the airspeed keeps falling

body.p: Proper pitch control required for continuously decreasing airspeed is the subtle skill in this Task. As airspeed decreases in a climb, the pitch attitude tends to lower unless the pilot increases elevator pressure [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. In the second 90°, rolling out increases the vertical component of lift, but the speed keeps falling, so a slight increase of back pressure is still needed to keep the pitch from decreasing [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

bullets: Near the critical angle of attack the controls are less effective: the elevator is less responsive and larger movements are needed [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].
Feel: less resistance on the controls, bigger movements for the same response, and a slower reaction [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
Hearing: the sound of the airflow changes as speed decreases [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
In a power-on stall entry, most airplanes need the elevator progressively further back with right rudder as the airspeed decreases [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. The chandelle finish lives just short of that.

body.p: So 'hold the pitch constant' does not mean 'hold the yoke still'. The learner holds the picture of the nose against the horizon, and the back pressure keeps growing to hold it. Two opposite errors show up: the nose sags in the rollout (more airspeed at the end than planned), or the nose keeps rising (error 6, speed gone early) [[24:215|AFH 10-6]] (application for the sag).

Finish and recovery: wings level at 180°, airspeed just above the power-on stall speed, the nose-high attitude held momentarily [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. Once in controlled flight, reduce the pitch and return to straight-and-level cruise [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. Lower the nose smoothly and slowly so airspeed can build; a pitch change that is too fast can cost altitude [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

callout.text: If a stall begins, recover at once: forward elevator to reduce the angle of attack and stop the stall warning, level the wings, coordinate with rudder, adjust power [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. Stalling at any point is a listed chandelle error [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

check.q: Your learner says, 'I froze the yoke at 90°, so the pitch stayed constant.' What do you correct?
check.a: With speed falling, a slight increase of back pressure is needed to keep the pitch from decreasing [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]; hold the attitude, not the control position.

chunks.title: Energy management: the plan behind the maneuver

body.p: Energy management means planning, monitoring and controlling altitude and airspeed targets, including preventing an irreversible deceleration or sink rate [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]. Mismanaging altitude and airspeed contributes to the three most common types of fatal accidents: loss of control in flight, CFIT, and approach-and-landing accidents [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].

In the AFH's model the throttle is the total energy controller and the elevator is the energy distribution controller; neither one controls altitude or airspeed by itself [[24:90|AFH 4-4]]. In a chandelle the throttle adds energy (thrust greater than drag) while the elevator moves stored airspeed into altitude. When energy is exchanged, altitude goes up as airspeed comes down [[24:88|AFH 4-2]].

Teaching it: the chandelle is the cleanest flight demonstration of energy exchange a learner will see, so name it as you fly: 'Throttle in, energy in. Nose up, speed into height. At 180° the speed tank is nearly empty.' The risk side is the same picture: the maneuver plans to arrive with almost no spare airspeed, so a bad plan in the first 90° is paid for at the end (application).

callout.text: The energy picture uses indicated altitude and indicated airspeed, not height above the ground [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]. A chandelle over rising terrain climbs on the altimeter while the margin above the ground shrinks.

check.q: In energy terms, what does each control do during a chandelle?
check.a: The throttle adds total energy and the elevator distributes it, trading airspeed for altitude [[24:90|AFH 4-4]] [[24:88|AFH 4-2]].

chunks.title: Rate and radius of turn with confined area operations

body.p: Rate and radius of turn: at a given bank, a slower airspeed gives a smaller radius and a greater rate of turn [[24:75|AFH 3-14]]. Rate of turn = 1,091 x tangent of bank / true airspeed in knots, and radius = true airspeed squared / (11.26 x tangent of bank) [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]].

head: 30° bank, example TAS (not from a POH)
Rate of turn
Radius

body.p: So in the first 90°, with the bank fixed and the speed falling, the turn keeps tightening and speeding up (application of the AFH rule). Learners who expect an even pace reach the 90° reference sooner than they planned, which is one reason error 5, not starting the recovery at the 90° point, is so common [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

Confined area operations: the PHAK canyon example shows that airspeed is the most influential factor in how much room a turn needs, and that pilots often steepen the bank when slowing down would have been better [[1:138|PHAK 5-41]]. When faced with rising terrain, manage energy to maximize gains, and a safer heading may also be an option [[24:88|AFH 4-2]]. Application: a chandelle ends nose high at almost no spare airspeed, which is a poor tool for escaping a valley.

callout.text: Ask the learner on the ground: 'If you had to turn around in a narrow valley, would you fly a chandelle?' The answer you want is slow down first and turn early, not a last-moment climbing turn (application).

check.q: Why does the chandelle's turn tighten during the first 90° even though the bank stays at 30°?
check.a: At a given bank, slower airspeed means a smaller radius and greater rate of turn, and the speed keeps decreasing [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].

body.p: The chandelle starts by clearing the airspace for traffic and hazards [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. The PHAK says clearing should precede all turns, chandelles named among them; learners at all levels should call out 'clear' left, right, above or below, and the pilot of a high-wing airplane raises the wing in the turn direction to look, a low-wing pilot lowers it [[1:364|PHAK 14-30]].

bullets: Scan in eye movements of no more than 10°, each area for at least 1 second [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
Clearing plus good scanning is the most effective collision avoidance strategy, and the instructor should insist on a clearing procedure [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].
Aircraft cluster near VORs and surface areas, and most collisions happen in good weather [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].
Practice areas can be crowded, and haze aggravates the hazard [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

body.p: Chandelle-specific blind spots (application): the nose rises high in the first 90°, hiding the sky ahead, and the turn covers half a circle while climbing into the airspace above. Have the learner check above as well as around, and keep scanning during the maneuver; not scanning is listed error 13 [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

Teach the habit, not just the call. Learners who think the instructor does all the scanning never build vigilance, and instructors were aboard in 37 percent of the midair collisions in one study [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Tell the learner you are both responsible for the lookout [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

check.q: Why should a high-wing learner raise the wing before rolling into a chandelle?
check.a: The high wing hides traffic in the turn direction; momentarily raising it lets the pilot look before turning [[1:364|PHAK 14-30]].

chunks.title: Low altitude, stalls, spins and uncoordinated flight

body.p: Low altitude maneuvering, including stall, spin, or CFIT, is why the ACS sets a floor: select an altitude that allows the maneuver to be performed no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (ACS AI.IX.C.S2). Figure 10-3 shows the same floor at the entry [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. The chandelle climbs, so the entry is its lowest point, and a shallow-dive entry [[24:214|AFH 10-5]] ends lower than it began; plan from the highest terrain under the whole half circle (application).

bullets: Stall: knowing load factors and VA helps prevent stalls from steep turns or excessive maneuvering near the ground [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

Spin: holding uncoordinated control deflections can set up a spin, especially at low altitude [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]. A cross-control stall can come with little warning, roll toward inverted and be deadly close to the ground [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
CFIT: mismanaging altitude and airspeed is a factor in CFIT and loss-of-control accidents [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].
Teaching altitude: avoid creating a hazard by teaching at an inappropriate altitude, such as stalls with too little room to recover [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

body.p: Uncoordinated flight at the end of a chandelle is the risk to watch hardest. The airplane is slow, nose high, at high power, with the left-turning tendencies at their strongest and the rollout adding adverse yaw [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. If a stall comes while uncoordinated, the bank may change until the angle of attack is reduced [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. A ball well out of center in the last 45° of a left chandelle is your cue to coach 'right rudder' at once.

callout.text: Never let a learner practice chandelles low to 'see the ground better.' The maneuver's whole design is to finish near the stall.

check.q: Terrain under the practice area rises to 1,250 feet MSL. What is the lowest altitude any part of the chandelle may reach?
check.a: 2,750 feet MSL: 1,250 + 1,500 = 2,750, to stay no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (ACS AI.IX.C.S2).

chunks.title: Division of attention, distractions and disorientation

body.p: Division of attention between aircraft control and orientation: in one half circle the learner holds bank, builds pitch, adds power and rudder, tracks two references and scans for traffic while the speed falls. Two AFH errors are attention errors: not scanning for traffic, and performing by reference to the instruments instead of visual references [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

bullets: Fixation: absorption in one task, such as the airspeed indicator, while other parts slip; often a sign the task has had too little practice on its own [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].
Spot it by glancing at the learner's eyes; a gaze stuck on one instrument suggests fixation [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].

Task prioritization: before asking for several tasks at once, make sure each can be done reasonably well in isolation [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. Budgeting time and prioritizing tasks gives room to work without error [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

Loss of situational awareness: it includes knowing the airplane's position and other aircraft [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. In a chandelle that means knowing the heading to the 180° point and the height above the terrain.

body.p: Distractions: most stall/spin accidents happened when attention was diverted from flying, and the most effective training creates distractions while the learner practices maneuvers [[25:179|AIH 9-9]] [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. Choose them with care in a chandelle. Asking the learner to read the outside air temperature or identify a forced landing field is on the AIH list [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]; reaching into the back seat near the stall is not a fair test (application).

Disorientation: in visual conditions the eyes are the main orientation source and usually win over false body sensations [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]]. An abrupt head movement in a prolonged constant-rate turn can cause the Coriolis illusion [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]. Keep the learner's head movements smooth and the eyes outside.

callout.text: Priority to coach (application): outside attitude first, a quick glance at the airspeed and ball second, traffic scan throughout. Radio calls and checklists wait until the airplane is back in level flight.

check.q: Your learner's eyes stay on the airspeed indicator through the whole second 90°. What is the problem and how do you spot it next time?
check.a: Fixation, and flying by instruments instead of outside references, a listed error [[25:81|AIH 3-30]] [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]. Glance at the learner's eyes to see where they are looking [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].

body.p: Start only on solid fundamentals. Performance maneuver training should not begin until the pilot shows consistent competency in the basics; begin with a detailed ground lesson for each maneuver and use segmented building blocks with enough repetition [[24:210|AFH 10-1]]. For a chandelle the blocks are climbing turns [[24:81|AFH 3-20]], slow flight and power-on stalls [[24:116|AFH 5-11]] [[24:123|AFH 5-18]] (application: these are the skills the chandelle combines).

Ground lesson: the objective and standard, Figure 10-3, the two halves, the rudder story for left and right, the entry speed for today's weight, the sensations near the stall, the recovery, and who has the controls [[25:175|AIH 9-5]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. The AIH says to introduce anxiety-provoking maneuvers with care: explain the aerodynamics, describe the sensations to expect, cover the recovery, and treat fears as normal [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

head: Point in Figure 10-3
What you say while demonstrating (application from the AFH text)
rows: 'Clear left, right, above. Flaps up. Speed is our entry speed. My 90° reference is that hill, 180° is behind us.' [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]
'Thirty degrees of bank. Now smooth back pressure and power together. Watch the nose come up steadily.' [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]
'Bank stays at 30, I am holding it against overbanking. More right rudder as we slow.' [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]
'Highest pitch now. From here the nose stays right there and the bank comes out slowly.' [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]
'Same pitch picture, a bit more back pressure to hold it, and lots of right rudder in this left one.' [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]
'Wings level on the reference, just above the stall. Hold it. Now ease the nose down.' [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]

bullets: Demonstrate exactly the way you want it practiced, in the order you explained it, and explain power and attitudes as you fly; if the demo strays from the explanation, say so at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
Fly one each way. The ACS allows either direction (ACS AI.IX.C.S5), and the rudder work is different [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].
Segment it (application of the AFH's building blocks): a few first halves only, ending in a held pitch and a normal recovery, before the whole maneuver.
Have the learner talk you through one before flying it; a misunderstanding about the halves shows up before the learner is busy flying [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Integrate instruments: introduce the maneuver with outside and instrument references together [[25:181|AIH 9-11]], but keep the eyes mostly outside.

callout.text: With a potentially hazardous maneuver, be ready to take control at any time, especially on the learner's first attempts [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Guard the controls through the last 45°, where the stall, the left yaw and the overbanking all peak.

check.q: Before a learner's first chandelle, which earlier skills should already be consistent, and what source supports waiting for them?
check.a: Climbing turns, slow flight and power-on stalls (application); the AFH says performance maneuver training should not take place until the pilot shows consistent competency in the fundamentals [[24:210|AFH 10-1]].

body.p: The AFH lists 14 common chandelle errors [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]. For S9 the examiner may fly some of them as your learner: name what you see, explain the cause and give the fix.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Initial bank too shallow, resulting in a stall
About 30°; check the attitude indicator once after roll-in [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]
Initial bank too steep, failing to get maximum performance
Shallower bank; steep banks cut the rate of climb [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]
Bank increases after it is set
Bank creeping up as the speed falls
Not starting the recovery at the 90° point
Still at 30° past the wingtip reference
Pick and call the 90° reference before entry (application)
Pitch low on recovery, airspeed well above stall
Progressive right rudder as speed falls [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]
Recover at once [[24:125|AFH 5-20]], then fix the pitch plan
Steep turn instead of a climbing maneuver
Pitch and power, not just bank [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]
Scan as part of the maneuver [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]
Flying by instruments, not visual references
Outside references first; watch the learner's eyes [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]

body.p: Table errors: [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]; fixes as cited. Application on error 2: with a shallow bank the airplane turns slowly, so the speed runs out before the heading reaches 180°.

How to analyze: in the learner-tells, learner-does step you can tell whether an error comes from a misconception or from motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Safety permitting, let a learner go part of the way into a mistake and find the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]; in a chandelle, set your limit before the flight, such as the first stall warning (application). If a learner flies it well but you doubt the understanding, ask for a variation, for example a different bank or a right chandelle after only lefts [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

callout.text: Teach the priority: if the speed is nearly gone and the heading is short of 180°, lower the nose. A stall is a listed error [[24:215|AFH 10-6]], while a heading miss is a tolerance call (ACS AI.IX.C.S7).

check.q: The examiner, as your learner, finishes on heading with the airspeed well above the stall and the nose that sagged during the rollout. What do you say?
check.a: The pitch was low on recovery, so the speed stayed high [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]. Reach the full pitch by 90° and add slight back pressure in the rollout to keep the nose from dropping [[24:213|AFH 10-4]] [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

f1.caption: Figure 10-3. Chandelle. (AFH 10-5)
f1.alt: A high-wing airplane flies a climbing 180° turn over farmland toward hills, shown at five lettered points. A: level entry, with a box listing clear area, VA, VO or manufacturer's recommended speed, no lower than 1,500 feet AGL, trim. B: rolled into a bank, with a box listing roll into 30° bank, neutralize ailerons, begin increasing pitch toward climbing attitude, apply full power without exceeding limits, increase rudder pressure. C: banked and nose high, with a box saying maintain 30° bank until this point then begin gradual rollout, and maximum pitch should be reached, no further changes in pitch. D: shallower bank, box says continue smooth rollout, hold pitch, maintain coordinated flight. E: wings level and nose high, box says complete rollout to wings level at 180° point, airspeed VS1, maintain coordinated flight, hold airspeed without stalling.

f2.caption: Figure 3-12. The rudder opposes adverse yaw to help coordinate the turn. (AFH 3-13)
f2.alt: A high-wing airplane banked over a city and airport. The raised wing has a large arrow labeled more lift and the lowered wing a small arrow labeled reduced lift. A red curved arrow at the nose is labeled adverse yaw, a blue arrow at the raised wing is labeled additional induced drag, and a box says the rudder opposes adverse yaw to coordinate the turn.

f3.caption: Figure 5-51. Asymmetrical loading of propeller (P-factor). (PHAK 5-33)
f3.alt: Two side views of the nose of a high-wing airplane. Left, low angle of attack: the arrows for the load on the upward moving and downward moving propeller blades are equal. Right, high angle of attack with the nose raised: the arrow for the downward moving blade is much longer than the one for the upward moving blade.

f4.caption: Figure 3-15. Overbanking tendency. (AFH 3-14)
f4.alt: A high-wing airplane in a steep bank against the sky. A box at the raised outer wing says it travels a greater distance, with higher speed and more lift. A box at the lowered inner wing says it travels a shorter distance, with lower speed and less lift. A large curved arrow shows the bank tending to steepen.

f5.caption: Figure 5-7. Slow flight: low airspeed, high angle of attack, high power, and constant altitude. (AFH 5-11)
f5.alt: A high-wing airplane flying nose high against a blue sky with a yellow arrow showing its direction of flight. A box at the top reads slow flight, and text at the lower left reads low airspeed, high angle of attack, high power setting, and constant altitude.

f6.caption: Figure 3-14. Angle of bank and airspeed regulate rate and radius of turn. (AFH 3-14)
f6.alt: Two top-down panels of airplanes turning over green fields toward a runway marked 36. Left, constant airspeed: turns at 10°, 20° and 30° of bank, with the 30° turn the tightest; text says a larger bank gives a smaller radius and greater turn rate. Right, constant angle of bank: turns at 100, 90 and 80 knots, with the 80 knot turn the tightest; text says a slower airspeed gives a smaller radius and greater turn rate.

f7.caption: Figure 4-3. The reservoir analogy illustrating the primary role of the throttle and elevator to manage the airplane's energy state. (AFH 4-4)
f7.alt: A pipe diagram. Energy gain enters on the left through a valve labeled throttle as thrust, and energy loss leaves on the right as drag. A vertical pipe labeled net energy flow, thrust minus drag, leads down to a valve labeled elevator that connects two tanks: Altitude (potential energy) on the left and Airspeed (kinetic energy) on the right, with arrows showing flow both ways between them.

scenario.title: Introducing chandelles to a commercial student
scenario.setup: You are a CFI with a commercial student in a fixed-pitch, high-wing trainer on a warm afternoon. The student flies good climbing turns and power-on stalls but has never seen a chandelle. Two people and half fuel put the airplane well under maximum weight. The practice area lies over farmland at 1,100 feet MSL with a ridge to the north, and another school's trainers work the same area.

questions.q: The student briefs the max-weight VA from the POH as the entry speed. What do you teach?
questions.a: VA goes down as weight goes down [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]], and above VA the airplane can reach its limit load before it stalls [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. Use the POH entry speed or VA for today's lighter weight [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

questions.q: What altitude do you pick, and what about the ridge?
questions.a: At least 1,100 + 1,500 = 2,600 feet MSL for the lowest point, which is the entry (ACS AI.IX.C.S2) [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. Check the terrain under the whole half circle and turn away from the ridge; energy is measured on the altimeter, not above the ground [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].

questions.q: The student starts to roll in without looking. What do you do?
questions.a: Stop it and have the student clear the area aloud, raising the wing to look [[1:364|PHAK 14-30]]; any tendency to enter maneuvers without checking for traffic needs correcting at once [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

questions.q: On the student's first left chandelle the bank grows to 40° and the 90° point comes early. What is happening and what is your cue?
questions.a: The overbanking tendency increases as speed drops [[24:214|AFH 10-5]], and more bank turns the airplane faster [[24:75|AFH 3-14]]. Cue: 'hold the bank at 30 with a little opposite aileron.'

questions.q: In the last 45° the ball is far right of center, the horn chirps and the student is staring at the airspeed indicator. What are your priorities?
questions.a: Get coordination and angle of attack first: right rudder [[24:214|AFH 10-5]], and lower the nose if the stall warning persists [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. Then fix the attention problem: eyes outside, a glance inside [[24:215|AFH 10-6]] [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]. Be ready to take control [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

questions.q: On the debrief the student asks whether a chandelle is a good way to turn around in a narrow valley. What do you say?
questions.a: No. It ends just above the stall with almost no spare energy [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]; airspeed is the biggest factor in turn room, so slow down and turn early [[1:138|PHAK 5-41]], or take a safer heading [[24:88|AFH 4-2]].

skills.do: Clear the area, explaining the clearing calls and the wing raise or lower as you do them.
skills.practice: Clear before every practice chandelle and call it aloud; then have a mock learner do the calls while you watch their head move [[1:364|PHAK 14-30]] [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

skills.do: Select an altitude that allows the maneuver to be performed no lower than 1,500 feet AGL, and explain how you chose it.
skills.practice: Before each one, say the highest terrain elevation under the turn plus 1,500 feet, then add room for a shallow-dive entry [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

skills.do: Establish the appropriate entry configuration, power, and airspeed: flaps and gear up, POH speed or VA for the actual weight, explained as you set it.
skills.practice: Work out VA for each flight's weight and brief it aloud on the ground [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]] [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

skills.do: Establish the angle of bank at approximately 30°, explaining why not steeper.
skills.practice: Learn the 30° sight picture from the right seat and confirm it once on the attitude indicator [[24:214|AFH 10-5]] [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

skills.do: Simultaneously apply power and pitch for a smooth, coordinated climbing turn, in either direction, to the 90° point, with a constant bank and continuously decreasing airspeed, while explaining overbanking and the right rudder.
skills.practice: Fly the first half alone a few times, timing the pitch so the highest pitch arrives at the 90° reference [[24:213|AFH 10-4]] [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

skills.do: Begin a coordinated constant rate rollout from the 90° point to the 180° point, maintaining power and a constant pitch attitude, explaining the extra back pressure.
skills.practice: Narrate 'same pitch, rolling out, more back pressure' on every rollout until it is automatic [[24:214|AFH 10-5]] [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

skills.do: Complete rollout at the 180° point, ±10° just above a stall airspeed, and maintaining that airspeed momentarily avoiding a stall.
skills.practice: Know the POH power-on stall speed; have another pilot call your heading and airspeed at wings level [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

skills.do: Resume straight-and-level flight with minimum loss of altitude, explaining why the nose comes down smoothly.
skills.practice: Lower the nose slowly so airspeed builds before level flight; note the altitude change each time [[24:81|AFH 3-20]] [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

skills.do: Analyze and correct common errors related to this Task: watch a flawed chandelle, name the error, explain its cause, give the fix, and take control if safety requires.
skills.practice: Have a fellow applicant fly each AFH error on purpose while you diagnose it aloud [[24:215|AFH 10-6]] [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

quiz.q: What does the AFH say a chandelle is judged on?
options: Total altitude gained, compared with the POH climb chart for the day
Climb performance for the bank and power selected, and the skill shown
Reaching exactly VX at the 180° point with the wings level
Finishing within 50 feet of a target altitude set before entry
quiz.why: Not altitude gained, but proficiency in maximizing climb performance for the power and bank selected, and the skill demonstrated [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

quiz.q: In the second 90°, the rollout increases the vertical component of lift. What else does the pitch need?
options: A slight decrease of back pressure to keep the nose from rising
No change at all, since the yoke is held where it was at 90°
A slight increase of back pressure as the speed keeps falling
Nose-down trim so the pitch drops to the level-flight picture
quiz.why: As speed continues to decrease, a slight increase of elevator back pressure keeps the pitch from decreasing [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

quiz.q: Rolling out of a right chandelle, what rudder does the AFH describe?
options: Very little left rudder, or less right rudder, depending on the airplane
Significant right rudder, more than a left chandelle's rollout needs
Full left rudder, held from the 90° point all the way to wings level
No rudder at all, since the ailerons alone keep the airplane fully coordinated
quiz.why: Rolling left out of a right chandelle yaws the nose right and partly cancels the left-turning tendency [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

quiz.q: What happens to the overbanking tendency as the chandelle's airspeed decreases?
options: It decreases, so the learner can neutralize the ailerons
It reverses and the bank tends to shallow out
It stays the same as in any medium-bank turn
It increases, so aileron holds the bank until 90°
quiz.why: As airspeed decreases the overbanking tendency increases; proper aileron use keeps the bank fixed until the rollout [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

quiz.q: With a fixed-pitch propeller, how does the AFH say to set the throttle in the chandelle?
options: At idle, so the climb is driven only by the entry airspeed
So that rpm limits are not exceeded
At the level cruise setting used for the entry, unchanged
Full throttle, ignoring rpm, for maximum performance
quiz.why: In airplanes with a fixed-pitch propeller, the throttle is set so as to not exceed rpm limitations [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

quiz.q: Which AFH chandelle error leads to a stall?
options: An initial bank that is too steep
Leveling the wings before the 180° point
An initial bank that is too shallow
A pitch attitude that is low on recovery
quiz.why: Error 2: initial bank too shallow resulting in a stall [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

quiz.q: What does the PHAK give as a rough VA for an older airplane with no published VA?
options: About 1.3 times the normal stall speed
About 1.7 times the normal stall speed
Exactly the never-exceed speed less 20 percent
About 2.5 times the normal stall speed
quiz.why: For older general aviation airplanes VA is approximately 1.7 times the normal stalling speed [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

quiz.q: At a constant 30° bank, what does a falling airspeed do to the turn?
options: Larger radius and slower rate, so the 90° point comes late
No change, since bank alone sets radius and rate
Larger radius but faster rate, as lift is lost
Smaller radius and greater rate of turn
quiz.why: At a given bank, slower airspeed gives a smaller radius and greater turn rate [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].

quiz.q: In the AFH energy model, what does the elevator do in a chandelle?
options: Adds total energy to the airplane
Moves energy from airspeed into altitude
Removes energy as drag
Controls altitude independently of airspeed
quiz.why: The elevator is the energy distribution controller [[24:90|AFH 4-4]]; trading airspeed for altitude, altitude goes up as airspeed comes down [[24:88|AFH 4-2]].

quiz.q: Which sensory cue does the AFH list for an approaching stall?
options: Controls getting heavier with quicker response
Engine rpm rising sharply at a fixed throttle
A steady drop in oil pressure as the airflow noise grows
Less control resistance, bigger movements needed
quiz.why: Feel: progressively less resistance, larger control movements needed and a slower response [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

final_quiz.q: During S9 the examiner, as your learner, flies a right chandelle from 030. Wings come level on 200, just above the stall, holding it a moment without stalling. What do you call out?
options: Out of tolerance: the heading was 10° short of the 210° target point
Out of tolerance: the target was 180, not 210
Within tolerance only because it was a right chandelle
Within the ±10° tolerance; 200 is exactly 10° short of 210
final_quiz.why: 030 + 180 = 210. The standard is the 180° point ±10° (ACS AI.IX.C.S7), so 200 to 220 passes. Debrief the early rollout anyway: the rollout rate decides the heading [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's chandelles always end 15 to 20 knots above the stall, on heading. Which correction do you coach?
options: Roll out faster in the second 90° so the speed drops sooner
Use a steeper initial bank of about 45° to slow down sooner
Raise the pitch more in the first 90° so maximum pitch at 90° is higher
Reduce power at the 90° point to bleed the extra airspeed
final_quiz.why: If the pitch is set too low, the airspeed never decreases to just above stall speed [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]; pitch low on recovery is a listed error [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

final_quiz.q: Halfway to 90° in a left chandelle the bank has crept from 30° to 40°. What two effects should you explain to the learner?
options: The turn rate increases and the climb performance decreases
The turn rate decreases and the climb performance increases
The stall speed decreases and the turn radius increases
Nothing changes as long as the pitch keeps rising smoothly to 90°
final_quiz.why: More bank at the same speed gives a greater rate of turn [[24:75|AFH 3-14]], and steep banks significantly decrease the rate of climb [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]. Allowing the bank to increase is a listed error [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

final_quiz.q: On a light day your learner wants to enter at the max-weight VA from the POH because 'faster means more energy.' What is the best reply?
options: Agree, because extra speed means extra margin and more altitude gained at the end
Agree, because VA does not change with weight in light airplanes like this trainer
Disagree, but only because the faster entry makes the turn radius larger
Disagree: VA drops with weight, and above it the limit load can come before the stall
final_quiz.why: VA goes down as weight goes down [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]; above VA or VO the airplane can reach its design load limit at less than the critical angle of attack [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner pulls up hard at the entry and the altitude gained is less than on gentler tries. Why?
options: Gentler pull-ups use less fuel, so the engine makes more power
A pull-up over about 2 G gains less, and may even lose altitude
A hard pull lowers the stall speed and wastes the airspeed
Hard pull-ups only matter in airplanes with constant-speed propellers
final_quiz.why: A chandelle pull-up with more than 2 G will not gain as much altitude and in low-powered airplanes may give a net loss; the smoothest pull-up gains the most [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

final_quiz.q: In the last 45° of a left chandelle the ball is well right of center and the airplane is near the stall. What is the main risk, and what do you coach?
options: A skid from too much right rudder; coach left rudder and more back pressure to hold the nose up
No real risk, since the wings are almost level; coach the learner to keep the pitch frozen
An uncoordinated stall that may change bank; coach right rudder, and lower the nose if the stall warning persists
An overspeed; coach a power reduction and a faster rollout to reach the 180° point sooner
final_quiz.why: Ball right of center in a slow left yaw needs right rudder [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. An uncoordinated stall may change the bank until the angle of attack is reduced, and recovery starts with forward elevator [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

final_quiz.q: You want a realistic distraction during chandelle practice. Which choice fits best?
options: Ask the learner to reach into the back seat for a chart near the 180° point
Drop a pencil on the floor during the rollout of a left chandelle
Ask the learner to read the outside air temperature during the first 90°
Ask the learner to retune the radio with eyes inside through the whole turn
final_quiz.why: Reading the outside air temperature is on the AIH list [[25:180|AIH 9-10]] and needs little head movement; abrupt head movements in a prolonged turn risk the Coriolis illusion [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].

final_quiz.q: Terrain in the practice area peaks at 1,850 feet MSL and your learner plans a shallow-dive entry. What is the lowest altitude the entry may reach?
options: 3,350 feet MSL, which keeps the dive no lower than 1,500 feet AGL
2,850 feet MSL, which keeps the airplane 1,000 feet above the highest terrain
3,350 feet MSL, but only for the 180° point of the maneuver
1,500 feet MSL, measured from sea level
final_quiz.why: 1,850 + 1,500 = 3,350 feet MSL. The whole maneuver stays no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (ACS AI.IX.C.S2), and a shallow-dive entry [[24:214|AFH 10-5]] makes the start the lowest point.

final_quiz.q: Your learner flies perfect left chandelles every time but you doubt the understanding. What does the AIH suggest?
options: Have the learner vary the performance slightly, for example a right chandelle
Sign off the maneuver now, since consistent performance is all the ACS ever measures
Demonstrate it again three times without the learner flying
Assign only a written test on the AFH chapter
final_quiz.why: When a learner may perform correctly without understanding, require them to vary the performance slightly or combine it with other operations [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

final_quiz.q: Why is a chandelle a poor way to reverse course in a narrow canyon?
options: Because the bank of 30° is too steep for any canyon, whatever the speed
Because a climbing turn always needs more room than a level turn at any bank
It ends near the stall with little spare energy; slowing first shrinks the turn far more
Because the AFH forbids climbing turns below 1,500 feet AGL at all times
final_quiz.why: The chandelle ends just above stall speed [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. Airspeed is the most influential factor in how much distance a turn needs; reducing speed is often better than steepening the bank [[1:138|PHAK 5-41]].

final_quiz.q: Figure 10-3 says to neutralize the ailerons after rolling in. A learner does that and the bank steepens near 90°. How do you explain the conflict?
options: The figure is right; the learner must have used rudder against the turn
Neutral works at the roll-in, but overbanking grows as speed drops, so aileron is needed
The bank steepens because of P-factor, which only rudder can correct
The figure applies to low-wing airplanes only, so ignore it in high-wing trainers
final_quiz.why: The AFH text says the overbanking tendency increases as airspeed decreases, so proper aileron use keeps the bank fixed until the rollout [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

final_quiz.q: A learner rolls out of a left chandelle with the wings level on the heading, but you watched the nose climb steadily all through the rollout. What happened, and what was the likely result?
options: Pitch rose during the rollout, so speed ran out early
The pitch was correct; a rising nose is part of the second 90°
The rollout was too slow, so the turn passed 180°
The bank was too steep at entry, so the heading was missed
final_quiz.why: Allowing the pitch attitude to increase as the bank is rolled out is a listed error [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]; pitch set too high can lead to a stall before completion [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

final_quiz.q: On the first attempt your learner reaches the stall warning at 150° with the nose high and does not lower it. What do you do?
options: Let it run to a full stall so the learner feels the result
Talk the learner through holding the pitch until 180°
Add full right rudder and keep holding the pitch so the heading reaches 180°
Coach forward elevator at once, and take control if there is no response
final_quiz.why: Recover by reducing the angle of attack to stop the warning [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. On a first attempt at a hazardous maneuver, be ready to take control at any time [[25:178|AIH 9-8]], and announce 'I have the flight controls' [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

takeaways: CFI standard: about 30°, wings level at 180° ±10°, just above a stall airspeed held a moment, no lower than 1,500 feet AGL, demonstrated while explaining.
First 90°: constant bank, rising pitch, highest pitch at 90°. Second 90°: constant pitch, constant-rate rollout.
Right rudder grows as speed falls; a left chandelle's rollout needs the most, a right one's needs less.
Overbanking grows as speed drops; hold the bank with aileron until 90°.
Enter at the POH speed or VA for today's weight, and pull smoothly; a hard pull costs altitude and invites an accelerated stall.
Hold the pitch picture, not the yoke: back pressure keeps increasing as the speed decays.
Teach it in blocks on solid fundamentals, guard the controls in the last 45°, and spot errors by the bank, the pitch timing, the ball and the learner's eyes.
cfi_notes: The PHAK calls the chandelle 'a maximum performance climbing turn' that ends 'at the minimum controllable airspeed', and says the aircraft 'is in a steep climbing turn and almost stalls' [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]] [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]]. The AFH says the bank is 'generally 30°' and the finish is 'just above the power-on stall speed' [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]; the CFI ACS says 'approximately 30°' and 'just above a stall airspeed' (ACS AI.IX.C.S4, S7). Teach the ACS wording for the checkride and the AFH for the how-to; the PHAK line is a loose description, not a bank or speed target.

Figure 10-3 says 'apply full power without exceeding limits' and 'airspeed VS1' [[24:214|AFH 10-5]], while the AFH text says the recommended power setting (cruise or climb for a constant-speed propeller) and just above the power-on stall speed [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. Teach the text and the POH, and never teach 'at' the stall speed as the target.

Figure 10-3 says 'neutralize ailerons' after the roll-in, but the same page says the overbanking tendency increases as speed decreases and aileron holds the bank [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]. Explain both: neutral at first, opposite aileron as it slows.

PHAK 5-37 says no combination of maneuver and gust can cause damage below maneuvering speed [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]], but PHAK 5-35 says VA does not protect against multiple full inputs in one axis or full inputs in more than one axis [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. Teach the more restrictive wording.

With a non-crewmember aboard, no intentional maneuver may exceed 60° of bank or 30° nose up unless everyone wears an approved parachute; flight tests and required maneuvers given by a CFI are excepted [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307]]. No source gives a chandelle pitch, so a commercial learner who practices with a passenger aboard should know this 30° nose-up limit applies if the pitch would exceed it.

The AIH distraction list includes dropping a pencil and getting something from the back seat [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. In a chandelle that ends near the stall, use those only in straight flight; use low head-movement distractions during the maneuver because of the Coriolis illusion [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].

The AIH lets a learner go part of the way into a mistake only 'safety permitting' [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Decide before the flight where your line is in a chandelle (for example the first steady stall warning) and brief it (application).

Parallax from the right seat, the exchange of controls and the general demonstration-performance flow are covered in the Steep Turns lesson (AI.IX.A). In a chandelle, the pitch picture you see from the right seat will not match the learner's, so coach from the attitude indicator and the learner's references (application).
gaps: No source gives a target pitch attitude, a typical altitude gain or a time for the chandelle; the pitch is found by flying, and the entry speed and power come from the POH/AFM [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].
The sources give no formula for VA at a lower weight; they only say it goes down, with a 100 versus 90 knot example [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]. Use the POH.
The amount of right or left rudder in each chandelle is airplane specific; the AFH says 'depending on the airplane' [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].
No source says how close to the stall a CFI should let a learner go before taking control in a chandelle; the AIH only says 'safety permitting' [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].
The AFH does not say whether to retrim during the chandelle; Figure 10-3 lists trim only at the entry [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

activities.title: True or false: pitch and the finish
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Holding a constant pitch in the second 90° means holding the yoke still.
cards.why: False. A slight increase of back pressure is needed to keep the pitch from decreasing as speed falls [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

cards.s: Near the critical angle of attack the elevator is less responsive and larger movements are needed.
The chandelle should end at the stall speed, with the stall warning steady.
cards.why: False. It ends just above the power-on stall speed, and stalling at any point is an error [[24:214|AFH 10-5]] [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

cards.s: Vision alone is a foolproof stall cue, because the nose is always high at the stall.
cards.why: False. An airplane can stall in any attitude, so vision is not foolproof [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

cards.s: After the finish, lowering the nose slowly lets the airspeed build and limits the altitude lost.
cards.why: True. A pitch change made too fast, before the airspeed increases, can cost altitude [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

cards.s: As airspeed decreases in a climb, the pitch tends to rise on its own.
cards.why: False. It tends to lower unless elevator pressure is increased [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

activities.title: Work the numbers you will brief
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Rate of turn at 30° of bank and 100 knots TAS?
Rate of turn at 30° of bank once the speed has dropped to 60 knots TAS?
items.why: 1,091 x 0.5774 / 60 = 10.50° per second. Same bank, slower speed, faster turn [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]] [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].

items.q: Turn radius at 30° of bank and 65 knots TAS?
An airplane stalls at 50 knots at 1 G. About what is its stall speed in a level 30° bank? (load factor 1 / cos 30°)
items.why: 1 / cos 30° = 1.155. Square root = 1.075. 50 x 1.075 = 53.7 knots; stall speed rises with the square root of load factor [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].

items.q: An older airplane with no published VA stalls at 55 knots. What is the PHAK's rough VA?
items.why: 1.7 x 55 = 93.5 knots [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. Use the POH where it gives one.

items.q: Highest terrain under the turn is 1,320 feet MSL. Lowest altitude the chandelle may reach?
items.why: 1,320 + 1,500 = 2,820 feet MSL, no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (ACS AI.IX.C.S2).

activities.title: A chandelle lesson, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are a CFI with a commercial student in a fixed-pitch trainer, light today. The student has never flown a chandelle.

steps.s: On the ground the student says the chandelle is 'a steep turn where you pull up.' What do you teach first?
options: The two halves: constant bank with rising pitch, then constant pitch with a constant-rate rollout
The entry speed only; the rest is learned in the air by feel
The steep turn procedure at 50° of bank, adding climb power
Nothing yet; demonstrate first and explain after landing
steps.why: The AFH describes the chandelle in two phases [[24:213|AFH 10-4]], and performance maneuvers start with a detailed ground lesson [[24:210|AFH 10-1]]. Flying it as a steep turn is a listed error [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

steps.s: Airborne, you demonstrate a left chandelle and the airspeed at 180° ends 15 knots high because you were talking. What now?
options: Say nothing; the student did not notice
Acknowledge it at once, explain why (pitch low at 90°) and fly it again
Tell the student it was correct
Skip the right chandelle demo to save time
steps.why: If the demonstration does not closely conform to the explanation, acknowledge and explain the deviation at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]; pitch too low means the speed never decays [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

steps.s: On the student's first try the bank creeps to 40° before 90°.
options: Coach: hold the bank at 30 with a little opposite aileron
Coach: add left rudder to stop the turn
Coach: more back pressure to raise the nose faster
Let it go; bank does not matter in the first half
steps.why: The overbanking tendency increases as speed drops; aileron keeps the bank fixed until 90° [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

steps.s: Late in the rollout of the left chandelle the ball is far right and the stall horn starts.
options: Coach more left rudder to center it
Coach right rudder and, if the warning stays steady, lower the nose
Hold everything to make the heading
Add left aileron to finish the rollout faster
steps.why: The left chandelle rollout needs significant right rudder [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]; recovery starts by reducing the angle of attack to stop the warning [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

steps.s: At 160° the warning is steady, the nose is still high, and your 'nose down' call gets no reaction.
options: Wait and see if the stall breaks cleanly
Take control and say 'I have the flight controls'
Pull with the student to hold the nose
Reduce power and hope the nose drops
steps.why: Be ready to take control on a first attempt at a hazardous maneuver [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]; take the controls and calmly announce it, without fighting the learner [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
